Female Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii) extrude fertilised ova that are notably small, with an average egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters. This modest oocyte size yields a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], placing the species at the lower end of the size spectrum among viviparous scorpaenids. The tiny, yolk-dependent embryos develop within the ovarian cavity, relying entirely on maternal provisioning during the initial months of gestation. Following eclosion, the prolarvae emerge as lecithotrophic, non-feeding individuals that subsist on endogenous yolk reserves until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. This brief endotrophic phase is typical of temperate rocky-reef species that produce large numbers of small offspring as a bet-hedging strategy in a variable coastal environment. The relatively low investment per individual larva is offset by a compensatory mechanism: females release a very large quantity of larvae during each spawning event, thereby increasing the probability that at least some recruits will encounter favorable settlement conditions on shallow reef habitats.

Field records of the reproductive biology of this species reveal that, under thermal regimes characteristic of autumn spawning aggregations along the Korean Peninsula (12 °C [T = 12 °C]), individual females produce approximately 780,000 larvae per spawning season [Ri = approximately 780,000 larvae per spawning season], a value that reflects an extreme r-selected strategy within the otherwise K-selected Sebastes genus. This massive larval output, sustained through a spawning period extending several weeks, represents one of the highest fecundities documented among sympatric Sebastes species and reflects an adaptive strategy to offset high larval mortality in the pelagic environment. The protracted release of larvae over many days rather than a single massive pulse likely improves the temporal match between larval presence and peaks in planktonic prey availability. Such a strategy, combined with the large number of small larvae produced, enables Korean rockfish to maintain stable recruitment even in years when oceanographic conditions are suboptimal, a life-history feature that has contributed to its success as both a dominant reef predator and a target of coastal fisheries across its range.

The species demonstrates a moderate growth trajectory that culminates in an ultimate total length of approximately 65 centimeters [Li = approximately 65 centimeters], a size attained only after many years of somatic investment in the cold, productive waters of the northwestern Pacific. Males and females exhibit similar asymptotic lengths, though females tend to achieve slightly larger maximum sizes, likely as a consequence of the energetic demands associated with vitellogenesis and gestation. Juveniles recruit to shallow, structured habitats such as rocky crevices and macroalgal beds, where they feed on small crustaceans and rapidly accumulate mass during their first few years of life. The growth pattern follows a decelerating curve typical of long-lived temperate scorpaenids, with the most rapid increases occurring during the first five to seven years before approaching the asymptotic length. At 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], the species ranks among the larger members of the subgenus Sebastodes, with only a few congeners exceeding this size in adjacent waters.

Puberty in this species is initiated when individuals reach a total length at puberty of 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters], a threshold that typically corresponds to an age of three to four years depending on local thermal and nutritional conditions. This length-based onset of maturity is a common pattern among iteroparous rockfishes, ensuring that females have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the high energetic cost of gestation and larval production before initiating reproductive activity. Reaching 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters] in total length signifies the transition from the immature juvenile phase to the reproductively viable adult stage, triggering gametogenesis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Individuals that achieve this size earlier in the season generally produce their first brood during the following autumn spawning period. Populations inhabiting warmer southern waters may reach this pubertal length slightly faster than those from colder northern ranges, although the length threshold itself remains remarkably consistent across the species' geographic distribution, suggesting strong genetic canalization of this trait.

The maximum lifespan of Korean rockfish has been estimated at 20 years [am = 20 years] for individuals reared under natural thermal conditions averaging 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a longevity that is among the highest recorded for the genus in the Northwestern Pacific, reflecting the stable, low-mortality environment of deep reef habitats. This longevity is consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of temperate Sebastes species, which generally combine late maturity, extended reproductive lifespans, and iteroparity to buffer against years of poor recruitment. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum asymptotic length is approximately 3,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,100 grams], a body mass that reflects the substantial accumulation of somatic tissue over two decades of sustained feeding on fish, squid, and large benthic crustaceans. The demographic profile that emerges from these values — a 20-year maximum lifespan (20 years) [am = 20 years] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] and a ultimate body mass of 3,100 grams [Wwi = 3,100 grams] — renders the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing of reproductive adults, a conservation concern that has prompted management measures across its range.
